EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“How does the transferability of human capital across different tasks affect workers’ wages and employment opportunities?”

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  

Method: Difference-in-Differences (event-study augmented) combined with a shift–share (Bartik-type) instrument.

Rationale  
a) The German economy experienced large, well-dated, exogenous shocks in task demand driven by ICT diffusion and organizational change (mid-1980s robots/CNC, early-1990s PC & networking, late-1990s ERP).  
b) These shocks were heterogeneous: occupations with a high ex-ante share of routine, codifiable tasks were hit hardest, whereas non-routine analytic and interactive tasks were little affected.  
c) The IAB data give long worker panels, letting us difference out permanent worker heterogeneity with individual fixed effects and compare wage (or employment probability) trajectories before and after the shock.  
d) To isolate exogenous variation, we build a shift-share “Routine Task Intensity shock” (RTI_shock) for each occupation–year:  

 RTI_shock_ot = (Routine share_o,1980) × (National fall in routine tasks_t)  

Workers in occupations above the median RTI_shock in a given period are “treated.” The shock is predetermined from a 1980 base year, making it exogenous to subsequent worker behaviour.  

Formal equation (event-study form):  

 y_iot = Σ_τ≠−1 β_τ · Treated_o × 1{t=τ} + γ_i + δ_t + θ_o + X_itΨ + ε_iot  

where y = log real wage or employment dummy; γ_i = worker FE; δ_t = year FE; θ_o = occupation FE.

We will also use the continuous RTI_shock as an instrument for individual task switching (first stage) to estimate the causal impact of actually changing task mix on wages (second stage).

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated_iot = 1 if occupation o’s RTI_shock_t is in the top quartile (or above median) of the distribution in year t; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Workers in occupations whose RTI_shock_t is in the bottom quartile (or below median) in year t. They serve as the counterfactual evolution of wages absent a large task shock.

Treatment timing / event date  
The “event” starts in 1985 (robotics/CNC) and again in 1993 (PC diffusion). In the DID we stack two four-year windows around each shock; in the event-study we define τ=−6,…,+10 relative to the first year the occupation’s RTI_shock enters the top quartile.

No running variable ⇒ no RDD.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Parallel trends: Absent the task shock, wages of high- and low-RTI occupations would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Germany’s strong wage-setting institutions generated similar growth rates before ICT diffusion; we test this visually and with pre-trend placebo coefficients.

A2. Exogeneity of RTI_shock: The 1980 routine share is predetermined; national falls in routine tasks are driven by technology, not local demand.  
Plausibility: Germany imports technology innovations; occupation routine share originates in historical task content, largely fixed pre-ICT.

A3. Stable composition/sec. shocks: No other contemporaneous occupation-specific reforms differentially affect treated vs control groups.  
Plausibility: No major occupation-specific regulations coincide with both shocks; we add occupation×time-varying controls (union coverage, industry demand) to mitigate.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  

T1. Differential pre-trends or anticipation.  
  • Graph & test event-study τ<0 coefficients.  
  • Vary pre-period baseline year (1978 vs 1980).  
  • Synthetic-control re-weighting of controls to match pre-trends.

T2. Selective worker mobility (sorting into future low-shock occupations).  
  • Include individual fixed effects and occupation×year FE.  
  • Instrument actual task change with RTI_shock (2SLS); robustness: restrict to stayers (no occupation change five years pre-shock).

T3. Measurement error in task content.  
  • Use two alternative task dictionaries (Autor-Handel routines vs German BIBB survey).  
  • Attenuation bias → demonstrate stability of β across measures.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)  

```r
# -------- 0. Packages ----------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast fe regressions
library(ggplot2)
library(ivreg)        # 2SLS for robustness

# -------- 1. Load Data ----------
worker <- fread("iab_worker_panel_1975_2001.csv")          # yearly worker spells
task   <- fread("occupation_task_content_1980.csv")        # routine share_1980
nat    <- fread("national_routine_share_change.csv")       # Δ routine nationally

# -------- 2. Construct Shock ----------
# merge baseline routine share
worker <- merge(worker, task[, .(occupation, routine80)], by="occupation")

# merge national change
worker <- merge(worker, nat, by="year")   # variable: nat_dRoutine

# shift-share shock
worker[, RTI_shock := routine80 * nat_dRoutine]

# treatment dummy (top quartile each year)
worker[, quartile := cut(RTI_shock,
                         breaks = quantile(RTI_shock, probs = 0:4/4, na.rm = TRUE),
                         labels = 1:4, include.lowest=TRUE),
       by = year]
worker[, treated := as.integer(quartile %in% c(4))]

# event time relative to first treatment exposure
# year when occupation first enters Q4
first_treat <- worker[treated == 1, 
                      .(t0 = min(year)), by = occupation]
worker <- merge(worker, first_treat, by="occupation", all.x=TRUE)
worker[, event_time := year - t0]

# -------- 3. Main DID / Event-study ----------
# keep window -6 … +10 around first treatment
est_sample <- worker[event_time >= -6 & event_time <= 10]

# event-study regression
es_formula <- feols(log_wage ~ i(event_time, treated, ref = -1) + age + tenure
                    | id + year + occupation,
                    cluster = "occupation", data = est_sample)

etable(es_formula)

# -------- 4. 2SLS robustness: task switch ----------
# First-stage: probability of changing main task
worker[, switched_task := shift(task_code, 1L) != task_code, by = id]

fs  <- ivreg(log_wage ~ switched_task + age + tenure |
                         RTI_shock + age + tenure, data = worker)
summary(fs)

# -------- 5. Parallel trend check ----------
coefplot <- coefplot(es_formula, 
                     keep = "event_time::treated",
                     ci = 0.95) + 
            geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype="dashed") +
            ggtitle("Event-study coefficients")
print(coefplot)
```

Robustness check displayed: 2SLS and alternative task dictionary (not shown due to brevity).

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Economic theory (specific vs general human capital):  
• Workers whose skills are highly task-specific and whose tasks become obsolete will suffer wage declines and higher separation risk unless their human capital is transferable.  
Prior: Treated workers’ wages fall 4–7 log-points (≈ 4–7 %) within four years after the shock, relative to controls. Employment probability falls 2–3 p.p. Effect smaller (≈ 0) for workers with multi-task or broader vocational certificates.

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically confirmed ………………… 0.8  
C2: Exogenous treatment assignment (predetermined RTI, tech shocks) …… 0.8  
C3: No other differential shocks / SUTVA violations ……………………………… 0.6  
C4: Stable composition (worker FE; migration minimal) …………………………… 0.7  
C5: No anticipation or dynamic treatment bias ………………………………………… 0.6  

(Average ≈ 0.7 → reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.)

─────────────────────────────────────────────  
The plan delivers a transparent, testable research design linking exogenous variation in task demand to individual labour-market outcomes, allowing us to quantify the role of task-specific versus transferable human capital.
